episode_title: 218. Divorce Financial Mistakes: 10 Lessons You Should Know | Divorce Clarity Guide
question: What financial mistakes did Catherine Shanahan face in her own divorce despite being a financial planner?
transcript_excerpt: Although Catherine was in control of the financial life during her marriage and there was no financial discrepancy between the spouses, she discovered her divorce agreement was not written strong enough to protect her. Years later, this led her back into the courtroom for the first time—not to get divorced, but because her agreement lacked proper legal language and protections, forcing her to defend herself against post-divorce claims.

episode_title: 218. Divorce Financial Mistakes: 10 Lessons You Should Know | Divorce Clarity Guide
question: How does My Divorce Solution's Financial Portrait process help clients make better divorce decisions?
transcript_excerpt: The MDS Financial Portrait helps people understand their financial choices while they still have the opportunity to make them by incorporating historical context and providing the right information to evaluate decisions. The process includes gathering and reviewing documents, identifying gaps, explaining connections, and doing modeling scenarios so clients understand the real-life impact of keeping assets like the house versus negotiating away retirement savings.

episode_title: 218. Divorce Financial Mistakes: 10 Lessons You Should Know | Divorce Clarity Guide
question: Why do most divorce cases not require attorneys to exchange the same documents twice during financial discovery?
transcript_excerpt: Catherine and Shalhoub argue that in most cases, spouses will voluntarily provide information when given the opportunity and benefit of the doubt. Only a small percentage of people refuse to give information, and those are the cases that end up going to trial. The redundancy of having two attorneys collect the same documents is inefficient, yet remains standard practice in family law.

episode_title: 218. Divorce Financial Mistakes: 10 Lessons You Should Know | Divorce Clarity Guide
question: What is the difference between an amicable divorce and being financially informed in divorce?
transcript_excerpt: Amicable means staying out of court and not fighting, but does not automatically mean you are financially informed. One party may say 'I will take care of you' without providing supporting documentation or helping you understand what assets and debts are actually divided. Being financially informed requires documented knowledge of what you are receiving and what it means for your post-divorce life, even if the process remains amicable.

episode_title: 218. Divorce Financial Mistakes: 10 Lessons You Should Know | Divorce Clarity Guide
question: How can small legal details in a divorce agreement create major financial problems years later?
transcript_excerpt: Catherine's personal example: she remained on the deed of the marital home after divorce but never forced her ex-spouse to refinance or remove her name. When he later became angry and threatened to sue her over an unrelated matter, she discovered she was still legally liable for the house and any mortgage debt, despite being financially stable at signing. Details about property transfers, business ownership, and post-divorce responsibilities must be addressed immediately, not deferred.
